content: {"id": "f834f739-4462-4759-9965-125fbbc951ea", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
{"id": "9e244bc2-6813-483a-8ee8-fccc52d59366", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "ALB vs NLB Differences in Load Balancing"}]}

{"id": "90c8d4a4-2781-4baa-8899-fc1ec1df678f", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here is how the two compare.

| | **Application Load Balancer (ALB)** | **Network Load Balancer (NLB)** |
|---|---|---|
| **OSI layer** | Layer 7 (application) | Layer 4 (transport) |
| **Protocols** | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket | TCP, UDP, TLS, TCP_UDP, QUIC |
| **Routing** | Content-based: host, path, headers, query strings, HTTP method, source IP | Based on IP protocol data (port and protocol) |
| **Performance** | Good for web workloads. It inspects each request, so latency is higher. | Very high throughput and ultra-low latency. It handles millions of requests per second and sudden traffic spikes. |
| **IP addresses** | Dynamic. You use the DNS name. | One static IP per AZ, and you can assign Elastic IPs. |
| **Targets** | Instances, IPs, Lambda functions | Instances, IPs, and ALBs |
| **TLS** | Terminates TLS and can authenticate users with Cognito or OIDC | Can terminate TLS or pass it through to the targets |
| **Client IP** | Passed in the `X-Forwarded-For` header | Preserved at the network level for instance targets |
| **Extras** | Redirects, fixed responses, weighted target groups, sticky sessions, WAF integration | PrivateLink (endpoint services), and it is often used for static IP allow-listing |
| **Security groups** | Supported | Supported, though only if you attach them when you create the NLB |

**Choose an ALB when:**
- You run HTTP/HTTPS apps such as microservices, containers, or APIs.
- You need path-based or host-based routing.
- You want WAF, authentication, or Lambda targets.

**Choose an NLB when:**
- You need extreme performance or very low latency.
- You carry non-HTTP traffic such as gaming, IoT, or custom TCP/UDP protocols.
- You need static or Elastic IPs, for example for partner firewall allow-lists.
- You want to expose a service through AWS PrivateLink.

You can also put an NLB in front of an ALB. That gives you static IPs and PrivateLink while keeping Layer 7 routing.

NLB feature support, such as QUIC and security group handling, has changed over time. I can check the current AWS documentation if you need exact details for a design decision.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
